content: The B Strategy emphasizes the importance of providing treatment and patient support to all individuals diagnosed with tuberculosis (TB). The World Health Organization (WHO) has updated its guidelines to incorporate the best available evidence for treating drug-susceptible TB and ensuring comprehensive patient care. These updates aim to guide national TB control program managers, policymakers, and medical practitioners in making informed decisions across diverse geographical, economic, and social contexts. The updated guidelines for treating drug-susceptible TB and patient care have two primary objectives: 1. To provide revised recommendations based on newly available evidence regarding the treatment of drug-susceptible TB and patient care. 2. To summarize the changes in the new guidelines while consolidating all existing and valid WHO recommendations on the treatment of drug-susceptible TB and patient care. In July 2016, the WHO convened a meeting of the Guidelines Development Group (GDG), which consisted of external TB experts from various disciplines. The purpose of this meeting was to review evidence on key aspects of drug-susceptible TB treatment and patient care and to formulate recommendations for updating the fourth edition of the TB treatment guidelines, originally published in 2010. The scope of the 2017 update included revising evidence-based policy recommendations from 2010 and adding new GRADE-based recommendations on patient care, regardless of whether the disease was drug-susceptible or drug-resistant. This included reviewing the model of care for patients with drug-resistant TB to assess the quality of available evidence. Before the meeting, the WHO Steering Committee identified key questions, which were extensively discussed during four online meetings with GDG members. These questions were structured using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes) format to facilitate systematic reviews by research teams. During this time, the American Thoracic Society (ATS), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) were also developing new clinical practice guidelines for drug-susceptible TB treatment, with WHO staff contributing to this effort. The evidence and materials were shared with reviewers from the University of California, San Francisco, and McGill University, who contributed to both the ATS/CDC/IDSA guidelines and the WHO guidelines. The GDG proposed several PICO questions for systematic reviews, focusing on priority areas of drug-susceptible TB treatment, such as: The effectiveness of 4-month fluoroquinolone-containing regimens compared to the standard 6-month regimen (2HRZE/4HR). The use of fixed-dose combination (FDC) tablets versus separate drug formulations. Dosing frequency (daily vs. intermittent). Antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and TB treatment duration for patients living with HIV. The effectiveness of adjuvant corticosteroids for TB pericarditis and meningitis. Management of patients requiring retreatment. Additionally, the GDG addressed priority areas of patient care, including: The effectiveness of treatment supervision and adherence interventions. Decentralized models of care for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). The recommendations were formulated using the GRADE approach, except for the Category II treatment regimen, where evidence was insufficient. In this case, a good practice statement approach was used. The guidelines were reviewed by an External Review Group comprising experts and end-users from all WHO regions. Key recommendations include: 1. Shortened fluoroquinolone-containing regimens: These should not replace the standard 6-month rifampicin-based regimen (2HRZE/4HR) for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB (strong recommendation, moderate certainty). 2. Fixed-dose combination (FDC) tablets: FDC tablets are recommended over separate drug formulations for treating drug-susceptible TB (conditional recommendation, low certainty). 3. Dosing frequency: Thrice-weekly dosing is not recommended during either the intensive or continuation phases of therapy. Daily dosing remains the preferred frequency (conditional recommendation, very low certainty). 4. ART for TB patients living with HIV: ART should be initiated in all TB patients with HIV, regardless of CD4 count (strong recommendation, high certainty). TB treatment should begin first, followed by ART within the first 8 weeks of TB treatment. For patients with CD4 counts below 50 cells/mm³, ART should start within the first 2 weeks of TB treatment. 5. TB treatment duration for HIV co-infected patients: A 6-month standard treatment regimen is recommended over extended treatment durations of 8 months or more (conditional recommendation, very low certainty). 6. Adjuvant corticosteroid therapy: For tuberculous meningitis, initial corticosteroid therapy with dexamethasone or prednisolone tapered over 6–8 weeks is strongly recommended (moderate certainty). For tuberculous pericarditis, corticosteroid therapy may be used (conditional recommendation, very low certainty). 7. Category II regimen for retreatment: The empirical use of the WHO Category II regimen is no longer recommended. Drug-susceptibility testing should guide the choice of treatment regimen (good practice statement). Patient care recommendations emphasize the importance of health education, counseling, and adherence interventions tailored to individual needs. Communityor home-based directly observed treatment (DOT) is preferred over health facility-based DOT or unsupervised treatment. Video-observed treatment (VOT) may replace DOT where feasible. Material and psychological support, as well as staff education, are also recommended to enhance treatment adherence. For MDR-TB, a decentralized model of care is recommended over a centralized model (conditional recommendation, very low certainty). National TB programs and public health leaders are urged to adapt these recommendations based on their country’s TB epidemic, health system strengths and weaknesses, and available resources. Careful adaptation is necessary to avoid undermining existing treatment programs, ensure access for vulnerable populations, and achieve sustainable impact. The guidelines reflect the current state of knowledge, and ongoing research will inform future updates.
